answers.a: Equiano saw the sea and a slave ship riding at anchor, waiting for its cargo. He was then handled and tossed up by the crew to see if he was sound.
answers.b: The crew handled Equiano and tossed him up to see if he was sound, the way a buyer inspects goods before a purchase. The ship waited for its cargo, and Equiano was part of that cargo, a person treated as a thing to be checked and sold.
answers.c: The ship waited at the African coast for its cargo of enslaved people, and its destination was the Americas, where plantation owners bought them. The trade moved people across the ocean from Africa to the Americas, linking the two continents in one system.

answers.a: The Navigation Acts forced colonial trade onto English ships and through English ports, and certain goods could be shipped only to England.
answers.b: The Acts kept colonial trade in English hands so that the profits and the customs revenue went to England, which is what mercantilism wanted: the colonies enriching the mother country.
answers.c: Because enforcement was loose, colonial merchants grew rich smuggling and colonial assemblies got used to managing their own affairs, which built habits of self-government.

answers.a: The chart shows the trade winds and the sailing courses from one continent to the other, mapping the Atlantic between the Americas, Europe, and Africa.
answers.b: Ships rode the trade winds west to the Americas and the westerlies home, so the sailing routes the chart maps followed the wind patterns.
answers.c: The chart shows routes and winds but no numbers, so it cannot show how much cargo or how many ships crossed the Atlantic; it shows the paths, not the volume of trade.

answers.a: One leg is the Middle Passage, carrying enslaved people from Africa to plantations in the Americas. Another is manufactured goods from Europe to Africa, and a third is plantation crops back to Europe.
answers.b: Sugar, tobacco, and rice plantations needed large workforces, so planters' demand for workers drove the Africa-to-Americas leg, and the profits from the crops paid for the next voyage.
answers.c: Warfare and kidnapping spread along the African coast as the trade destabilized African societies.

answers.a: The fur trade created new inequalities: villages that trapped beaver grew rich on European goods while villages that did not fell behind, changing old relationships between neighbors.
answers.b: Beaver populations declined near Iroquois territory as European demand for furs kept growing, so the Iroquois pushed into Huron territory to control the beaver trade.
answers.c: Measles and smallpox killed between half and two-thirds of the Huron after 1634, leaving Huron villages too weak to defend themselves when the Iroquois attacked in 1649.

answers.a: Rowlandson describes the attackers as hell-hounds and as wolves tearing sheep, as cruel, godless enemies rather than as human beings.
answers.b: Rowlandson wrote as a grieving captive who had just watched her neighbors killed, and for a Puritan audience that expected her suffering to prove God's providence, so she cast the war as Christians against heathens.
answers.c: Metacom was killed in August 1676 and many survivors were sold into slavery in the West Indies, which ended organized Native resistance in southern New England and cleared the way for English expansion.

answers.a: The image shows sickness and death at Jamestown: a sick settler is carried between two men, another sits dejected on a cannon, and a man digs a grave in the background.
answers.b: The settlers' weakness from sickness made them dependent on the Powhatan for corn, so early relations were shaped by dependence: the English needed Native food to survive.
answers.c: By the 1640s relations had changed to open war and English dominance: after the 1622 attack and a decade of war, the second war in 1644 ended with the Powhatan broken and confined to small reserves.

answers.a: The Catawba allied with the English, traded deerskins and food, and sent peddlers through the settlements selling pottery, baskets, and moccasins.
answers.b: Traders paid for Catawba goods with alcohol, smallpox epidemics cut their numbers, and by the 1750s the Catawba had temporarily given up their land and their status as a separate people.
answers.c: The Catawba chose adaptation and alliance rather than resistance, which let them survive as traders but cost them land and status; other peoples chose resistance, like the Pueblos in 1680, and won temporary independence. Native choices shaped the outcome.

outline.thesis: Transatlantic trade shaped the British colonies' regional economies to a great extent, but differently in each region: plantation staples in the South and Caribbean, mixed trade and shipping in New England, grain and trade in the middle colonies.
outline.context: The growth of the Atlantic economy under the Navigation Acts and the rise of plantation slavery.
outline.evidence1: Tobacco in the Chesapeake and sugar in the Caribbean and rice in South Carolina: staple crops grown for export on enslaved labor, dependent on English markets.
outline.evidence2: Fish and timber and shipbuilding in New England, and wheat in the middle colonies: diversified trade with the Caribbean and Europe.
outline.comparison: Trade made the South dependent on a single export and enslaved labor, while New England's trade diversified its economy, so the same Atlantic system produced different regional economies.
outline.complexity: Qualify by region and by other forces: geography and labor systems also shaped the economies, so trade was the driver but local conditions set the form.

outline.thesis: Interactions differed greatly among the three powers: Spain forced labor and missions, France built alliance-based fur trade, England planted settler colonies that pushed Native peoples off the land, though all three depended on Native peoples and brought disease.
outline.context: The different goals that brought each power to North America, and the Native societies already living there.
outline.evidence1: Spanish missions and the encomienda; French fur-trade alliances with the Huron; English settler colonies pushing Native peoples off the land.
outline.evidence2: All three powers depended on Native peoples for food, furs, or labor, and all three brought disease that devastated Native populations.
outline.comparison: The form of interaction differed, labor versus trade versus land, but dependence on Native peoples and the spread of disease were common to all three.
outline.complexity: Qualify by region and time: Spanish accommodation after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, and English praying towns alongside displacement, so the difference was uneven.
